deep.reconstruction:
The page is a continuation of a manuscript table of quadratic residues modulo primes. It covers p = 421, 431, 433 and 439; the previous page ends with 419 and the next page begins with 443.

Notation, inferred from the page and checked against the arithmetic:
- The sign written above each prime records p mod 4. It is + for p ≡ 1 (mod 4): 421, 433. It is − for p ≡ 3 (mod 4): 431, 439.
- For p ≡ 1 (mod 4), −1 is a residue, so r and p−r have the same character. The entry is therefore marked ∓ (i.e. ±) and only residues r ≤ (p−1)/2 are listed. For 421 this means residues in 1..210 (105 of them); for 433, residues in 1..216 (108 of them).
- For p ≡ 3 (mod 4), −1 is a non-residue, so the entry is marked + and all residues in 1..p−1 are listed. That is 215 residues for 431 (the list ends at 424) and 219 for 439 (the list ends at 436).

In modern terms, each line is the set {r : 1 ≤ r ≤ N, (r/p) = 1}, with N = (p−1)/2 for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and N = p−1 for p ≡ 3 (mod 4). How the lists were computed is not shown. They were plausibly built from squares together with multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol (or by quadratic reciprocity for prime arguments). The corrections bear this out: numbers were inserted above the line, and struck-through numbers were removed.

My spot checks (my own computations, using reciprocity):
- p = 421 (≡ 5 mod 8). Correctly 2 ∉ list, 3, 5, 7, 11 ∈ list, 13 ∉ list. The inserted 31 is correct: (31/421) = (18/31) = 1. The inserted 113 is correct: (82/113) = (41/113) = 1. The inserted 178 = 2·89 is correct: (−1)(−1) = 1. The list has exactly 105 entries, as it should.
- p = 431 (≡ 7 mod 8). The inserted 326 = 2·163 is correct: (163/431) = 1. The tail is consistent: 424 is a residue and 425–430 are non-residues.
- p = 433 (≡ 1 mod 8). The inserted 32 is correct. The overwritten 132 = 4·3·11 is a residue. 215 and 216 are residues.
- p = 439 (≡ 7 mod 8). The inserted 13, 26, 117, 121, 122, 123, 139, 140 are all residues. Struck entries such as 30/31 (between 29 and 32) and 47/48 (after 45) are non-residues, so the strikings are correct corrections.

The circled 7 is the folio number. The struck '40117' at the top right is probably an old shelf or inventory mark.
errors: No errors found in any spot check; the visible corrections all repair genuine slips.

Earlier slips appear in the 439 list as struck-out entries, e.g. near 30/31, 47/48, 124, 131/132, 134–136, 348–349, 356, 358–359, 376 and 381–390. These were apparently non-residues written by mistake and then removed, with the missing residues inserted above the line.

results.what: Table of quadratic residues modulo the primes 421, 431, 433, 439. Residues up to p/2 with ± for p≡1 (mod 4); all residues for p≡3 (mod 4).
results.modern_name: Table of quadratic residues / Legendre symbol values
results.usually_credited_to: Residue tables go back to Euler, Legendre and Gauss. Gauss's Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), Table II, gives residues for primes < 100; larger tables were made later by Jacobi (Canon arithmeticus, 1839) and others.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computational table of the kind Gauss is well known to have compiled while working on quadratic reciprocity and related topics. It extends the published DA tables to primes in the 400s, but contains no new theory.
